Newsflash Newsroom , 25.07.2026, 19:35 Drone. The Romanian authorities will share with their NATO and European Union allies the results of their investigations into the two incidents involving drones that illegally entered Romanian airspace on Friday and Saturday, acting foreign minister Oana Ţoiu has announced. She also said on X that the illegal violation of national airspace is a premeditated act. Earlier, speaking to Fox News, she said that Romania’s borders and its sovereignty are non-negotiable, and that the military and NATO air policing forces will continue to monitor the land border, the Danube river and the Black Sea. On Saturday morning, a drone was shot down 10 km from Sfântu Gheorghe, in the Danube Delta by the same F-16 pilot who had destroyed another drone on Friday in Buzău county (southeast). Investigators have already determined that the first drone was a Shahed unmanned aerial vehicle, a model used by Russia in strikes on Ukraine. Acting defence minister Radu Miruţă gave assurances that the Romanian Army is doing its best with the means available to limit and eliminate the threat posed by such incidents for the population. He pointed out the need for cheaper solutions than fighter-launched missiles to shoot down drones entering Romanian airspace, but this requires further equipping the army, and the production and procurement of such systems take at least 11 months. In Brussels, European Council President António Costa congratulated the Romanian authorities on their rapid and efficient response and gave assurances that the European Union would continue to strengthen its security and deterrence capabilities. Holidays. The majority of Romanians going on holiday this summer are choosing to stay in Romania, preferring short trips and organising their travel independently rather than using travel agencies. These findings come from a survey showing that 34% of respondents are heading to the seaside, while 32% are choosing the mountains. Only one in five Romanians will travel abroad. Over 43% of those surveyed can afford a holiday of just three to four days, with rest being the primary goal for more than half of them. More than 30% of respondents state they will combine business with pleasure, and 13% intend to visit tourist attractions, while only 1% of Romanians are going on holiday for shopping. Nearly 39% of Romanians said they would not be taking a holiday at all this summer. BBC Proms. The Ministry of economy, digitalisation, entrepreneurship and tourism in Bucharest is promoting Romania as a tourist destination on a special page included in the 85,000 official brochures for 63 of the BBC Proms concerts, the oldest and one of the most prestigious classical music festivals in the world and held every summer at London’s Royal Albert Hall. On August 5, Alexandra Dariescu will become the first Romanian female pianist to perform at the BBC Proms and the first Romanian musician to be part of the festival’s line-up in the last three decades. The concert’s special brochure, running in 1,200 copies, will feature not only the promotional page for Romania as a tourist destination but also a page dedicated to Romanian cultural diplomacy in the United Kingdom. Festival. Sighișoara, in central Romania, is playing host to the 31st edition of the Medieval Art Festival, the country’s longest-running event of its kind. Activities for visitors of all ages include knightly tournaments, medieval music and theater performances, parades, interactive workshops in glassmaking, pottery, tailoring, and engraving, fire-juggling demonstrations, and dishes inspired by local cuisine. Held within the only inhabited medieval citadel in Southeast Europe, the Medieval Sighișoara Festival takes place under the High Patronage of Her Majesty Margareta, the Custodian of the Romanian Crown. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/08/poland-k.text: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday and police bolstered security after six people were killed in a mass shooting in the southern city of Krakow that the government said was likely inspired by far-right ideology. Saturday's attack in the city's historic main square shocked a country that has prided itself on being safer than many of its Western European neighbors, deepening public concern following a string of school stabbings in October that officials linked to extremist content online. Sixteen people were wounded in the attack, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in a critical condition in hospital, local authorities said. Krakow's old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that attracts visitors from around the globe, and several foreigners were among the casualties. One of the people who died was identified as a British citizen and another as Austrian, while five foreign nationals from Austria, Germany, Portugal, Russia and Britain were among the wounded. Three bodies, guns found at suspect's home In the suspect's hometown, Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski, about 200 km (124 miles) north of Krakow, police later found the bodies of his parents and sister at his home. Prosecutor's Office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was "highly likely" that the killings in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski and Krakow were carried out by the same person, but that investigations were ongoing. The three bodies found there had gunshot wounds, and seven firearms and a "significant" quantity of ammunition were recovered from the property, Prokopowicz added. Some nationalist politicians questioned a statement by Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski on Saturday that the attack was likely inspired by far-right ideology. "If Kierwinski has misinformed the public, he should face political consequences. We demand immediate explanations and access to information what he had based his statements on," Przemyslaw Czarnek, deputy head of the conservative opposition PiS party, wrote on X. The suspect belonged to a shooting club, but little more information about him has come to light so far. Streets closed as mourners leave candles In Krakow, the old town's main market square — one of Europe's largest medieval squares — and the surrounding streets remained closed, with police allowing only essential workers to pass. Many nearby cafes were closed and flags at the city hall were at half-mast. Mourners placed candles in several locations in the area. The traditional hourly trumpet call from St Mary's church on the square was suspended for 12 hours to commemorate the dead, the first time this has happened since 1939, state news agency PAP reported. In the capital, Warsaw, police said on Saturday they were strengthening security measures in busy areas popular with tourists. Barriers were installed on streets leading onto the Krakowskie Przedmiescie street in the historic heart of the capital. Attacks shake sense of security In Krakow, locals and tourists spoke of their shock on Sunday. "This is terrible for me, that (this) can happen in Poland because it's never happened like this in Poland... I think that this can be a new era in my country," local resident Witold Slowikowski said. In Warsaw, Maria, a 20-year-old cafe employee, said she "almost burst into tears" when she heard about the shooting. "Recent events — not just this one, but things happening lately — are really affecting our sense of security," she said. Leading daily newspaper Rzeczpospolita said in an editorial that the mass shooting brought a "brutal end to an era in which Poland was considered an island of safety." Officials and members of the public also praised the actions of police officers who apprehended the gunman, who was armed with a semi-automatic rifle. The two officers, who sustained gunshot wounds while overpowering the gunman after a close-range shootout, have regained consciousness, a regional government official told a press conference. Both had undergone surgery. Prime Minister Donald Tusk praised their bravery. "They likely saved many human lives, disregarding the risk to their own," he said on Saturday in a post on X.
